title: Microstructural Analysis of BaTiO3: Influence of the Barium Precursor and HCl Treatment
content: Barium titanate (BaTiO3) has been a ceramic material of great importance in electronics-related technologies [1]. Its wide range of applications is due to its outstanding properties, such as high permittivity, ferroelectricity, and piezoelectricity [2, 3]. This material is typically synthesized using a variety of solution-based methods, many of which result in BaCO3 impurities in the final product. It has been reported that such impurities appear either as a discrete phase or as a surface layer [4]. In this study, a microstructural analysis of BaTiO3 was performed using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) with a JEOL 7600. The research focused on evaluating the effect of post-synthesis treatment through HCl washing, as well as the impact of replacing the barium precursor. A synthesis using Ba(OH)2 was compared to another in which this precursor was changed by BaCl2. Through micrographic analysis, the influence of these modifications on the material’s morphology and structure was examined. The powders were synthesized by mixing the chemical reagents [CH3(CH2)3O]Ti (≈98%), C₆H₁₅NO3 (99.90%), and barium hydroxide Ba(OH)2·8H2O (≈98%) under an argon atmosphere with low humidity. The resulting gel was heated in an autoclave at 160°C for 20 hours and then dried at 80°C for 24 hours. After synthesis, a washing treatment with 10% HCl was performed for 2 hours to remove BaCO3. A second sample was prepared under the same conditions, replacing the Ba(OH)2·8H2O precursor with BaCl2·2H2O (≈99%) and adding NaOH (≈98%), without applying an additional acid washing treatment. Figure 1a shows the powders obtained before washing, where spheroidal particles of approximately 100 nm in diameter can be appreciated, along with additional structures exhibiting different morphologies and substantially greater scale. After HCl treatment (Figure 1b), a predominant presence of spheroidal particles can be observed, suggesting that the larger structures were primarily composed of BaCO3. On the other hand, when using BaCl2 as the barium precursor, smaller spheroidal particles (20-30 nm) forming agglomerates were obtained, as observed in Figure 1c, in conjunction with a visible absence of the larger structures associated with BaCO3. Changing the barium precursor is an alternative approach to obtaining BaTiO3 purer powders with finer nanostructures.
